This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which found no division-specific legal, incident or enforcement signal: its 2024 share of national LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases was 2.64% (Movilh regional table). Its recorded case trend follows the national one, which rose in 2025 to a record; a low share is not evidence of safety — most regions outside the two biggest rose that year.

There is no region-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding for this division; its recorded profile comes from the shared national case table. National frame: 2025 produced a record 3,620 discrimination cases on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression (+27.1%; 23% of all cases in 24 years), and 2024 was the first regression since the return of democracy. Protective national framework (Gender Identity Law 21.120 in force 2019, same-sex marriage 2022, anti-discrimination law 21.220) sits against concrete 2025-26 rollback (PAIG excluded from the 2026 budget; health-ministry circular N8 restricting PAIG for minors; legislative initiative CEI-57) and administrative document friction from Registro Civil identification-system issuance failures (Comptroller Final Report 264/2025), which is directly relevant to a traveller whose documents must match presentation.
visible.tangentialFactors: National frame applies: Movilh records LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases rising in this region during 2025 alongside the national increase; a recorded-case rise is adjacent to trans risk via general hostility but is not a visitor-specific exposure.
visible.localsOnly: Resident-facing: Gender Identity Law 21.120 name/sex rectification (12,669 people by Dec 2025; only 15.7% of adults who declared trans/non-binary in the 2024 census; the nonbinary X marker still requires a judicial process) and the PAIG gender-identity support programme removed from the 2026 budget affect residents, not visitors.

sources.claim: Chile country dossier (Outright International, published March 12, 2026) contains no Los Lagos-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding, which is the basis for this record's national-score assessment: same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; the hate-crime law has covered sexual orientation and gender identity since 2012; legal gender recognition by self-determination since 2019; a third sex option on birth certificates since 2006; and the 2025-26 rollback in which the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children. The dossier itself carries no division-specific information.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) supplies this record's division-specific figures from its national regional table: Los Lagos is placed at 3.14% of nationally documented abuse cases, the fourth-largest regional share, with a +9.09% year-on-year rise in 2025. Nationally, the report records a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025 (+27.1%, the highest in 24 years), with only Valparaiso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) falling while the other 14 regions rose; it reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which is what this record's mid-share reading rests on. The 2024 share cited in this record's comparison is not reproduced in this 2025 edition.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview for Chile (last updated 12 March 2026) is the national framework this region is assessed under: same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since March 2022, hate-crime law has included sexual orientation since 2012, a 2019 self-determination-based gender-recognition law is in force with a third sex option for intersex children on birth certificates, and in 2025 a criminal court issued the country's first lesbophobic-femicide conviction under Article 390 ter of the penal code. The 2025-26 rollback the record relies on is documented here: Congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, and a parliamentary commission's report approved in May 2025 - following the UK Cass Report - portrays gender-affirming initiatives as a threat to children's development and recommends restricting access. No Maule-specific content appears.

Movilh XXIV Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity in Chile (facts 2025, published March 2026): the national annual history of LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases, including the per-region case-share table used here and national totals — 3,620 recorded cases in 2025 (+27.1%, highest on record; 23% of all cases in 24 years), 2,847 in 2024 (+78.7%, the first regression since the return of democracy) — plus the 2025-26 national rollback (PAIG removed from the 2026 budget, health-ministry circular N8 restricting PAIG for minors, legislative initiative CEI-57 against trans children's rights).

Wikipedia's Chile country overview dates the national framework every regional visitor stands under: Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018, operative 2019) lets transgender people aged 14 and over change their name and sex on all official documents without requiring therapy or sex-reassignment surgery; the anti-discrimination law enacted in 2012 (Zamudio Law) protects sexual orientation and gender identity, extended to gender expression in 2018, and allows citizens to file anti-discrimination lawsuits; same-sex marriage and joint adoption by same-sex couples have been legal since 10 March 2022 (law approved 9 December 2021), following the 2015 civil union. It independently confirms the record's national-frame claims (Gender Identity Law 21.120 in force 2019, marriage since 2022, anti-discrimination law) with dates and a document-change mechanism directly relevant to a traveller whose identity papers must match their presentation.

visible.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88 — after Lima's 12, level with Lima Norte), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average — a materially concerning concentration not explained by population alone, and placing the unit below the national score (0.36).

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (regional session 3 September 2024, approved 6 September 2024, published in El Peruano November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people — their right to formal, dignified work in equitable conditions without discrimination on gender identity or expression, and recognition of the trans community as a vulnerable group. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it), but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion — the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (now 0.38, above national): La Libertad's per-capita lethality remains worse, though Lima's higher absolute count and 2025 reporting case have lifted its score since the original comparison. vs Tacna (0.34): both are modestly below national, but La Libertad's multi-year dataset is more robust evidence than a single incident.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2012–2021 LGTB homicide dataset (88 deaths) is majority gay men (55.8%); trans women account for 36.4% (about 32 cases). The regional concentration is real for trans people but the headline count is LGB-heavy — a rater should read the trans share directly rather than inherit the total.
visible.localsOnly: The regional labour-inclusion ordinance (Ordenanza 009-2024-GRLL-CR) protects resident workers in formal employment; a visitor does not use it.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Community self-governance (rondas campesinas dispute-resolution authority in parts of the department) is structural context relevant to general order, not trans-specific: no documented trans case involving it. General crime and political instability affect all travellers; the assessment reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Public Prosecutor's Office (Ministerio Público) news note of 23 March 2022 on its Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru 2012-2021: 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects; 58% of deaths concentrated in six fiscal districts - Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6) - placing La Libertad second in absolute count (level with Lima Norte) behind Lima. The study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and monitoring systems.

Regional Government La Libertad norms page for Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (6 September 2024): approves promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region, declaring that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognising the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad. The cached page carries only this normative header (title, date, operative sentence) with the full text linked as PDF; it directly evidences the record's claim that this regional council legislated for trans labour inclusion.

Official-gazette record (El Peruano, publication date 07/11/2024) of Ordenanza Regional N.° 000009-2024-GRLL-CR, presented in the regional council's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024: Its object is positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in La Libertad - the right to formal, dignified, productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code (discrimination as a crime), recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, recommends local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo); it enters into force the day after publication in El Peruano.

visible.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.
visible.tangentialFactors: A national law enacted in 2025 restricts entry to public bathrooms according to sexual orientation; being national legislation it applies in this department too and is a direct visitor-facing hazard for gender-nonconforming travellers.

sources.claim: Wayka (27 May 2025): Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a hostel room in Tacna on 19 April 2025, the autopsy recording death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways, after entering the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone about two hours later; the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime - an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Context offered: Peru has no gender-identity-recognition legislation and no law sanctioning hate crimes, and activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal (congressman Alejandro Muñante) restricting access to public bathrooms by sexual orientation; the Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021 (most victims gay men 55.8%, trans women 36.4%).

Trome (updated 21 May 2025): a 48-year-old trans woman was found dead inside the 'Los 5 Titos' hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna after entering on a Sunday with a man who later left alone carrying a white bag; she was initially processed as NN until identified through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route; relatives denounced the crime and demanded police action. The body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired; no suspect had been identified in the audited text.
